8. Star variability analysis. For any periodic variable star, the period is one of the most important
and most informative of its observable parameters. Studying the periods of variable stars, and
their changes in periods is an important part of the analysis of variable stars. If a star is perfectly
periodic, then every period is exactly the same. In that case we can predict its cycles in
advance.

8.1. Any perfectly periodic star with epoch time to (the time of maximum (or minimum) for
cycle number zero) and period P, shows its next maximum at time tp + P. This maximum time is
known as calculated-time of maximum (or minima) for cycle number опе (Сл).

Using this pattern write an equation for the calculated-time of maximum (Cj) for any cycle
number n of a perfectly periodic star with a period of P and epoch of to

8.2. The table 8 lists times of minima of an eclipsing binary star which has epoch:
to = JD 2442502.726 (JD: Julian Date) and period: P = 0.971534 day. Substituting these values
to the equation you wrote above, compute the calculated time of minima for each cycle of the
table and fill the “JD-Calculated” column of the table.

8.3. Fill the “(O-C) (in days)” column of the table. (O-C = observed value minus calculated
value)

8.4. Convert (O-C) values that you calculated in previous chapter into minutes and fill the
“(О-С) (in minutes)” column of the table.

8.5. Using the data of this completed table, construct (O-C) (in minutes) graph vs the
number of cycle and fit a trend line for your plotted data. (Graph papers are provided. Use
maximum range of the graph paper).

8.6. According to your results mention whether this star is perfectly periodic, almost periodic
or not periodic. Write English words:

“(1) perfectly periodic’, “(2) almost periodic” or “(3) not periodic’.
